outcome: No source I could open shows the Erdős–Oler equality (the optimal side for n−1 unit circles equals that for n, for triangular n) proved or refuted for any n ≥ 21 since 26 January 2024; the only in-window candidate is a self-hosted 'proof' reported for December 2024 that I could not read, and the n ≤ 15 instances (n = 6, 10, 15) were settled between 1987 and 1997.
problem_asks: One universal claim over the infinite family of triangular numbers n = k(k+1)/2 (k ≥ 2). For each such n: the smallest equilateral triangle that holds n−1 non-overlapping unit-radius circles has the same side length as the smallest that holds n. Unpacked: (a) s(n−1) ≤ s(n) is immediate by deleting one circle from the optimal hexagonal packing of n circles, so the conjectural content is the lower bound: no equilateral triangle smaller than the n-circle triangle holds n−1 circles. (b) It is claimed for every triangular n; no finite set of cases settles the bullet. Presupposed but not asked: the value s(n) itself, which the bullet takes as known. The Friedman page's formula for that side is 2(k−1)+2√3 under unit radius, so for n = 6, 10, 15, 21 the sides are 4+2√3, 6+2√3, 8+2√3, 10+2√3. The bullet does not ask whether a minimiser for n−1 must be the deletion configuration.

events.what_happened: Milano (1987) is the source that Friedman's 'Circles in Triangles' page gives for the optimal side of 4 and 5 unit circles in an equilateral triangle (s = 4√3 for 4; s = 4 + 2√3 for 5). I found no other source for this 1987 result and did not read the paper.
events.delivers: Per Friedman's page only: the optimal side for 5 unit circles is 4 + 2√3. Together with the 6-circle value 4 + 2√3 (Oler/Groemer 1961, per the same page) this is the Erdős–Oler equality for triangular n = 6 (s(5) = s(6)). Restricted to n = 6.
events.remains: The equality for every other triangular n: n = 10, 15, 21, 28 and all larger. The n = 3 case (2 circles versus 3) is not covered by any source I read.
events.directly_checkable: The 5-circle configuration with side 4 + 2√3 is explicit and can be drawn; the lower bound is the content and I did not check it.
events.doubts: Known to me only from Friedman's attribution. The primary paper was not read. Friedman's attributions for other n conflict with Wikipedia's (see disputes).
events.direction: Confirms the instance n = 6 of the conjecture (s(5) = s(6)). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Norman Oler, 'A finite packing problem', Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 4(2): 153–155, issue dated May 1961 (DOI 10.4153/CMB-1961-018-7; the Cambridge page says 'published online 20 November 2018', a digitisation date). Secondary sources say this paper settles the optimal packing of triangular numbers of circles in an equilateral triangle, and that the Erdős–Oler conjecture first appeared in or around this work: arXiv 2104.09324 (Problem 4, 'quickly solved for any triangular number n (citing Oler, 1961)'), Wikipedia, Friedman's page and arXiv 2212.12287. I could read only the Cambridge introduction, not the theorem.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources: for every triangular n = k(k+1)/2 the optimal packing of n unit-radius circles is the triangular piece of the hexagonal packing, side 2(k−1)+2√3 (Friedman's formula). Per arXiv 2212.12287 (which cites Oler), Oler also proved N ≤ (2/√3)A(Π) + ½P(Π) + 1 for disks in a polygon Π, which the authors describe as a tighter inequality; that it is tight at triangular N is my inference and unchecked. Says nothing about n−1.
events.remains: The n−1 equality for every triangular n. This is the Erdős–Oler claim itself, which Oler's result does not address.
events.directly_checkable: The hexagonal triangular packing of n = k(k+1)/2 unit circles, side 2(k−1)+2√3, is explicit and can be drawn by hand. Its optimality (the lower bound) is the 1961 content, which I did not check.
events.doubts: The scope (triangular numbers only) is from secondary sources, not the paper. No re-derivation was found: later papers (Graham–Lubachevsky 2004; arXiv 2104.09324; arXiv 2212.12287) use the result as known.
events.direction: Confirms the n-circle side for triangular n. This is the upper-bound half of the conjecture's equality as applied to n, not evidence against the conjecture.
events.object: The explicit hexagonal triangular packing of n = k(k+1)/2 unit circles in an equilateral triangle of side 2(k−1)+2√3 (Friedman's formula). Its optimality is shown by a non-constructive bound (per arXiv 2212.12287, Oler's inequality), not by exhibiting any other object. Not checked by me.
people: Erdős (credited with the conjecture by Wikipedia and others)
Groemer (named by Friedman as co-credit for the 1961 triangular cases)

events.what_happened: Hans Melissen, 'Densest packings of congruent circles in an equilateral triangle', The American Mathematical Monthly 100(10): 916–925, 1993 (DOI 10.2307/2324212 per a search listing). Per secondary sources (Wikipedia's pre-July-2025 sentence 'Optimal solutions are known for n < 13'; Friedman's figure attributions; a search-snippet summary of a 2021 student paper) it gives optimal packings for 4 through 12 circles by partition and pigeonhole arguments. I could not open the JSTOR record.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources: the optimal side for 4 through 12 unit-radius circles. For the Erdős–Oler claim this gives the instance n = 10 (s(9) = s(10) = 6 + 2√3, where s(9) is credited to Melissen 1993 by Friedman). Does not reach n = 15 or any larger triangular number.
events.remains: The n−1 equality for triangular n = 15 and every larger triangular number.
events.directly_checkable: The 9-circle and 10-circle configurations are explicit and checkable. The optimality (lower bound) for 9 is the content; I did not check Melissen's argument.
events.doubts: The primary paper was not read. Its scope rests on Wikipedia's older sentence and on secondary summaries.
events.direction: Confirms the instance n = 10 (s(9) = s(10)). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Charles Payan, 'Empilement de cercles égaux dans un triangle équilatéral. À propos d'une conjecture d'Erdős-Oler', Discrete Mathematics 165/166 (1997): 555–565, DOI 10.1016/S0012-365X(96)00201-4, MR 1439300. The title names the Erdős–Oler conjecture. The sentence 'This conjecture is now known to be true for n ≤ 15.' is followed by reference [5], this paper, in the 20 January 2024 Wikipedia revision (oldid 1197491729) and in the March 2026 revision. A search-snippet summary of the ScienceDirect abstract says Payan treats k ≤ 4 and proves k = 5 (14 circles), with the method said to extend 'somewhat more laboriously' to k = 6. I could not open the paper: ScienceDirect and DOI links returned 403 or a redirect page.
events.delivers: Per the snippet summary of its abstract: the Erdős–Oler equality for triangular n = 15 (s(14) = s(15) = 8 + 2√3), with the k ≤ 5 range matching Wikipedia's 'n ≤ 15'. Wikipedia credits this paper for the 'n ≤ 15' sentence; the cited scope itself is not in any text I could read.
events.remains: The n−1 equality for triangular n ≥ 21 (k ≥ 6). The snippet summary says the method extends to k = 6 'more laboriously' but does not say this was proved.
events.directly_checkable: The 14-circle configuration with side 8 + 2√3 is the 15-circle hexagonal packing with one circle deleted, so it is explicit. The lower bound (no smaller triangle holds 14) is the content, which I did not check.
events.doubts: The n = 15 claim rests on Wikipedia's citation and one snippet summary of the abstract, not on the text. Friedman's page does not list n = 14 as proved: it says 'found by Erdős/Oler in 1961' (see disputes). No named referee or later verifier was found; later papers only cite the paper.
events.direction: If the snippet summary is right, confirms the instance n = 15 (s(14) = s(15)). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: R. L. Graham and B. D. Lubachevsky, 'Dense packings of equal disks in an equilateral triangle: from 22 to 34 and beyond', DIMACS Technical Report 94-43 (1994), published in Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 2 (1995) #A1, and posted as arXiv math/0406252 (12 June 2004). Gives best packings for 22 ≤ n ≤ 34 and conjectured optimal packings for seven further infinite classes. The abstract says: 'It has also been conjectured that d(n−1) = d(n) in this case', i.e. for triangular n. I read the DIMACS abstract and the arXiv abstract.
events.revisions: arXiv math/0406252 has one version (v1, 12 June 2004); EJC 1995 publication.
events.delivers: Restates the Erdős–Oler equality as a conjecture for triangular n. Its computed packings cover n = 27 and 28 (triangular 28 = 7·8/2, i.e. k = 7), and the abstract reports best-found packings for 22 ≤ n ≤ 34. The abstract I read does not say whether d(27) = d(28) was observed. Numerical belief only; no proof.
events.remains: All triangular n. Restatement and numerical belief do not settle any instance.
events.directly_checkable: The best-found packings for n = 27 and 28 are numerical (minimum centre distance to 15 digits). The packings are not described in the abstract I read.
events.doubts: The conjecture is a claim by the authors, based on their computations, and is not described as proved. Their seven other families are also conjectural.
events.direction: Restates the conjecture and gives numerical evidence for the k = 7 instance. No counterexample.
events.object: Best-found packings of 27 and 28 unit disks in an equilateral triangle, given numerically (the abstract does not describe the configurations). Not an existence proof and not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: Sándor P. Fekete, Sven von Höveling and Christian Scheffer, 'Online Circle Packing', arXiv:1905.00612 (submitted 2 May 2019). The Introduction (read in the HTML rendering) calls the Erdős–Oler problem 'a long-standing open conjecture by Erdős and Oler from 1961' about optimal packings of n unit circles in an equilateral triangle, 'which has only been proven up to n=15', citing Oler 1961 as reference [15]. The wording comes from a summarising fetch and is not character-verified. This is a status statement, not a new result.
events.delivers: Nothing new. A 2019 status statement: the conjecture is open and known up to n = 15. It shows the n ≤ 15 range predates the window and the Wikipedia 2025 edits.
events.doubts: The n ≤ 15 range is a secondary statement in this paper; it cites Oler 1961 and does not identify which work proves the cases up to 15.
events.direction: Status only: open in general, proved for n ≤ 15.

events.what_happened: Orgil-Erdene Erdenebaatar and Uuganbaatar Ninjbat, 'The smallest convex K-gon containing N congruent disks', arXiv:2102.02568 (submitted 4 February 2021; one version). Keyword list includes 'Erdős-Oler conjecture'. Section 4 states Conjecture 2: 'If n > 3 is a triangular number, then the smallest triangle containing n disks is the same as that containing n−1 disks', described as 'a new version of the long standing Erdős-Oler conjecture'. The authors call it conjectured. The fetched text says they prove the triangular cases n ∈ {3, 6} in their K-gon setting (Theorem 5(b)), with the rendering garbled.
events.delivers: Restates a variant. Conjecture 2 is for the smallest triangle containing n disks, not for the equilateral triangle as stated in the bullet, so it is a changed container class. Says it proves only n = 3 and 6 in its setting, which Melissen covers in the equilateral case. Nothing new on the Erdős–Oler equality.
events.remains: The equilateral equality for all triangular n beyond the cases already known; Conjecture 2 itself for all n > 3.
events.doubts: The claimed proofs for n ∈ {3, 6} are read from a garbled rendering and I could not verify Theorem 5(b). The authors say their approach 'stopped at m = 4'. Not an independent check of the bullet's claim.

events.what_happened: A short list of unsolved plane geometry problems, arXiv:2104.09324 (submitted 16 April 2021; v1 as displayed). Problem 4 asks for the smallest triangle holding n circles of radius 1. Its 'Erdős–Oler packaging problem' particular case is stated as: for triangular n, the smallest equilateral triangle packing n−1 circles of radius 1 and the one packing n are the same. The list says Problem 4 was 'quickly solved for any triangular number n' citing Oler (1961), presents the Erdős–Oler case as an open question of 'great interest', and cites Melissen–Schuur (1995) for up to n = 18.
events.revisions: v1 as displayed; no later version seen.
events.delivers: Nothing new. A survey statement that the Erdős–Oler case is open and that the triangular-number case of Problem 4 is solved (Oler 1961).
events.direction: Status only: the Erdős–Oler case is open; the triangular Problem 4 is solved.
people: Editor/author of the list (not identified in the text I read)

events.what_happened: Paolo Amore, 'Circle packing in regular polygons', arXiv:2212.12287 (submitted 23 December 2022; one version). A numerical study of packings in regular polygons. In the equilateral-triangle discussion, footnote 2 says it is known that the optimal configuration is triangular-lattice, that 'Oler [17] has conjectured that the configurations with N−1 disks are obtained from the former', and that the conjecture 'is sometimes also attributed to Erdös'. Footnote 3 says deleting a disk from a perfectly packed configuration 'appear[s] to be also optimal' for triangle and hexagon.
events.delivers: Numerical observation only. For triangular containers the paper reports that the N−1 configurations 'appear to be' optimal, based on its computations (up to 400 disks in the triangle per the abstract; which N were tested for this claim I did not confirm). Not a proof and not a claim of optimality for all n.
events.remains: All of the equality as a proof.
events.directly_checkable: The numerical configurations are reproducible, but the paper does not state which are checked against the conjecture.
events.doubts: Empirical only ('appear to be'). Footnote 2 treats the triangular-lattice structure as known without citing a proof.
events.direction: Numerical support for the equality; no counterexample reported.

events.what_happened: A self-hosted document titled 'Optimal Circle Packings for Triangular Numbers: A Detailed Mathematical Proof of the Erdős-Oler Conjecture' appears on ResearchGate (publication 387465203, titled '...For Paul Erdos and Norman Oler conjecture') and Academia.edu (id 129891186). I saw these only as search-result titles. Both host pages returned HTTP 403 to my fetches, so I did not read the text. A search-snippet summary attributes the document to Duy Tan Nguyen, dated December 2024 on ResearchGate and uploaded in 2025 on Academia. The same summary says the document defines the side length as the smallest integer m for which a triangular lattice with m points per side holds the circles, and claims that any circle can be removed, which would prove the conjecture. I could not confirm the author, date, or content beyond the titles. No arXiv listing was found.
events.delivers: If the summary is accurate, the claimed full result: for every triangular n, the smallest triangle holding n−1 circles is the same as the one holding n. As summarised, the side-length definition uses triangular lattices only, which by itself does not establish the lower bound for arbitrary (non-lattice) packings. I could not check this.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds. If the lattice-only argument is what the document contains, the non-lattice case would remain open. Not established either way.
events.time_since_posted: about 22 months, if the December 2024 date holds (unverified)
events.doubts: Self-hosted, not on arXiv, not in any journal, and no public engagement found in my searches. Author and date come from one summary and the host pages were unreadable, so I cannot see comments or versions. The summary's lattice-only definition is the specific doubt: the hard direction (no smaller triangle at all) is the one a lattice restriction does not obviously reach. No independent verification found.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture in full, if the summary is accurate.
people: Duy Tan Nguyen (name from a single search summary; unverified)

events.what_happened: Antal Joós, 'Packing 13 circles in an equilateral triangle', Aequationes Mathematicae 95(1): 35–65 (2021), per an arXiv bibliography (2308.16523). Secondary sources (a 2021 student paper, not opened) say the proof was reported in September 2020, and that it proves Melissen's 13-point conjecture using continuous functions and calculus. Not opened: Springer DOI guess returned 404.
events.delivers: The optimal side for 13 unit-radius circles. Not an Erdős–Oler instance: 13 is neither triangular nor one less than a triangular number. It is part of Wikipedia's later sentence 'optimal solutions are proved for n ≤ 15' (added July 2025), not of the Erdős–Oler sentence.

checked_by.qualification: Undergraduate author of a 2021 student paper in AJUR on packing thirteen points
checked_by.what_they_did: Reportedly discusses Joós's 13-point proof and proposes a discrete route for part of it. Known only from a search-snippet summary; I did not open it.

events.doubts: The September 2020 date comes from a secondary source. The journal record was not read.
events.direction: Confirms the 13-point optimum. Not relevant to the Erdős–Oler equality.

events.what_happened: J. B. M. Melissen and P. C. Schuur, 'Packing 16, 17 or 18 circles in an equilateral triangle', Discrete Mathematics, 1995, pp. 333–342 (volume 142 or 145; sources disagree). Gives new packings for 16, 17 and 18 circles, found by simulated annealing and quasi-Newton optimisation, per a search-snippet abstract. Cited in arXiv 2104.09324 and in Wikipedia's references. Not opened.
events.delivers: Packings (upper bounds on side length) for 16, 17 and 18 circles. None of these is an Erdős–Oler instance: 16–18 are neither triangular nor one less than a triangular number. Discounted neighbour.
events.doubts: Known only from snippets and citing papers. Volume number disagrees between sources.
events.direction: Not applicable to the Erdős–Oler instances. Neighbouring problem.

events.what_happened: Anshul Raj Singh, 'On a square packing conjecture of Erdős', arXiv:2601.22163 (submitted 10 January 2026; one version). Concerns f(n), the maximum total side length of non-overlapping squares or equilateral triangles packed in a unit square or unit equilateral triangle, and shows Erdős's f(k²+1) = k conjecture is equivalent to convergence of a series. I read the abstract page. It does not mention Erdős–Oler, circles, or triangular numbers in the abstract text. Full text not read.
events.delivers: Nothing on the Erdős–Oler claim. It is a different problem: packing squares or triangles by total side length, not unit circles by side of the container.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different problem that shares an Erdős name and equilateral triangles.

disputes.summary: Who proved the 14-circle case (the n = 15 instance). Wikipedia cites Payan (1997) for 'known to be true for n ≤ 15' (ref [5] in both the January 2024 and March 2026 revisions). Friedman's undated 'Circles in Triangles' page lists the 14-circle side 8 + 2√3 as 'found by Erdős/Oler in 1961' (not proved) and the 15-circle side as 'proved by Erdős/Groemer in 1961'. These cannot both be the source of a proof for 14 without further reading of Payan and Oler.

Who conjectured the n−1 equality. Wikipedia and arXiv 2104.09324 name Erdős and Oler. arXiv 2212.12287 says 'Oler has conjectured' and that the conjecture 'is sometimes also attributed to Erdös'. Friedman's page says 'Erdős/Oler'. arXiv 2102.02568 calls it the Erdős-Oler conjecture.

The optimal-packing sentence changed in July 2025. The 20 January 2024 revision says 'Optimal solutions are known for n < 13 and for any triangular number of circles'. Edits of 19 July 2025 changed this to n ≤ 15 and cited Payan for n = 14. The 'now known to be true for n ≤ 15' sentence about the conjecture was already present in the January 2024 revision, so the n ≤ 15 claim predates the window.

summary: I ran 43 searches (40 standard, 2 extended, and a name search) and opened 26 sources, including the Wikipedia article (March 2026), its history and its 20 January 2024 revision, arXiv HTML renderings for the 2019–2023 status papers, Friedman's 'Circles in Triangles' page, the DIMACS report for Graham and Lubachevsky, and the Cambridge page for Oler. I could not read the primary texts of Oler 1961, Melissen 1993, Payan 1997, Joós 2021, the Nguyen document or the Melissen–Schuur paper: the sources returned 403, 404 or binary PDFs, and their content comes from search snippets or secondary sources, which I say where it matters. The settled cases, as the sources describe them, are triangular n = 3, 6, 10 and 15 (equality for k ≤ 5): n = 6 through Milano (1987) and Oler/Groemer (1961) on Friedman's attribution, n = 10 through Melissen (1993), and n = 15 through Payan (1997) as cited by Wikipedia. All of these predate the window. Wikipedia's 'now known to be true for n ≤ 15' sentence was already in its 20 January 2024 revision, and the July 2025 edits changed only the separate optimal-solutions sentence. The n ≥ 21 instances are conjectural in every source I could open: Graham–Lubachevsky (1994) give numerical belief for n = 27 and 28, the 2019, 2021 and 2022 papers call the claim open or conjectured, and Friedman's undated page lists the 14-circle side as 'found' rather than proved. No source dated after 26 January 2024 that I could open discusses the conjecture except Wikipedia's 2025 and 2026 revisions, which still call it a conjecture. The in-window candidate is the Nguyen self-hosted document, reported as December 2024 with a claimed full proof and a lattice-only side-length definition. I could not read it, its author and date come from one summary, and I found no public engagement with it. Close calls: (i) whether Payan's paper proves the 14-circle case and only that (Wikipedia implies it; the scope rests on one abstract summary); (ii) whether the Nguyen claim counts as an in-window event at all, since its existence is known only from search titles and a summary. No AI system is named in any event. The AI search (queries listed below) found only square-container circle packing work (AlphaEvolve, a Discovery Loop paper, a Cognizant blog), an OpenAI result on unit distances, a Gemini paper on Erdős problems, and an unopened OpenAI 'ten advances' post that a secondary source says has no triangle item. None of these concerns equilateral triangles.
competing_reading: The Nguyen document, if accurate and general, would settle the whole conjecture inside the window, which would move the problem from 'open' to 'proved since 2024'. The reading that nothing has happened rests on three things: the document is unreadable to me and has no peer review or arXiv listing; it is described as using a lattice-only definition, which does not obviously cover the lower bound for non-lattice packings; and no public engagement with it was found. A second reading treats Wikipedia's 'known for n ≤ 15' as the actual status and the Payan citation as settling 14 (the n = 15 instance), while Friedman's page reads the same 14-circle packing as only 'found' by Erdős/Oler in 1961. Those two readings give different counts for the small cases.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The text and date of the Nguyen document (ResearchGate publication 387465203 and Academia 129891186 returned 403), and whether an arXiv or journal version exists; and whether its argument covers non-lattice packings. (2) The text of Payan 1997: its exact scope (k ≤ 5 or k ≤ 4 plus k = 5) and whether it proves s(14) = s(15) for all packings. (3) Oler 1961 in full: whether it proves s(n) for triangular n and whether it states the n−1 conjecture. (4) Melissen 1993 for n = 9 and the Milano 1987 paper for n = 5. (5) Friedman's page attributions, to settle whether 14 is proved or only found. (6) Any post-2024 paper citing or rebutting the Nguyen claim, or a Lean formalisation of the n−1 equality.
